subject: Executive Intelligence Brief | 2026-09-09 | Iran claims Hormuz strikes as CENTCOM denies + Kyiv pause ends + two Windows zero-days hit KEV
preheader: IRGC claims strikes on two US destroyers (CENTCOM calls it false) as Iran's Hormuz blacklist grows and oil holds near a 7-week high; Kyiv absorbs a mass attack as the capital-strike pause lapses; CISA adds two actively-exploited Windows zero-days plus N-able N-central to KEV.

barometer.reason: Claimed Hormuz strikes on US Navy ships (denied by CENTCOM) plus a resumed mass attack on Kyiv mark the sharpest 24h escalation on both fronts this cycle.
Two actively-exploited Windows zero-days (Update Stack, ALPC) plus N-able N-central added to KEV alongside a record Patch Tuesday.
Steam-catapult reversal for CVN-81 and new LASSO/Ku-band awards add fresh schedule and demand signals.
Rare-earth chokepoint and DPA-driven munitions expansion persist; the carrier-catapult reversal adds a new schedule/cost risk to shipbuilding.
Hormuz transit at a post-May low (~10 ships/day) as the blacklist grows; magnet exposure unchanged.
DoD's ChatGPT/Grok rollout on GenAI.mil proceeds with Claude still excluded; removal timeline unchanged.
New LASSO and Ku-band awards continue a steady demand base; no major new Golden Dome award this cycle.
CMMC internal determination now roughly four days out; no new substance.

bluf.what: Iran's IRGC claimed it struck two U.S. Navy destroyers and multiple oil tankers/vessels on 8 Sep in retaliation for prior U.S. strikes; U.S. Central Command publicly called the claim 'completely FALSE,' stating no U.S. warship was hit and all IRGC attempted attacks failed. CENTCOM separately said it had destroyed five more Iranian tankers in the latest exchange.
bluf.matters: A direct claim/denial dispute over an attempted attack on U.S. Navy vessels is a materially higher-stakes event than the prior mine-and-tanker pattern, regardless of whether the strikes actually connected.
bluf.changes: Raises miscalculation risk: Iran is now attempting (per its own claims) direct hits on U.S. warships, not just tankers.
bluf.needToKnow: Treat the strike claim as CLAIMED/UNKNOWN and the 'no hit' outcome as KNOWN via CENTCOM; both the attempt and the denial are independently significant.

bluf.what: Iran's Persian Gulf Strait Authority (PGSA) -- the body that has managed a Hormuz transit-permit regime since May 2026 -- has expanded its vessel blacklist to roughly 56-57 ships (from 45 on 24 Aug), and Hormuz commercial transit has fallen to about 10 ships/day, the lowest since May, as Brent crude holds near a seven-week high (~$99/bbl).
bluf.matters: Rezaei's 7 Sep 'exclusion zone' announcement is best read as toughened enforcement of an existing PGSA authority, not a wholly new legal instrument -- but the practical effect (falling transit, rising insurance/legal ambiguity) is real and measurable independent of the rhetoric.
bluf.changes: Confirms that risk-avoidance by commercial shippers is accelerating, not just diplomatic signaling.
bluf.needToKnow: Watch the blacklist count and daily transit volume as the two hardest indicators; both are moving in the same direction.

bluf.what: The 5 Sep, 3-day Kyiv-Moscow capital-strike pause tied to the Witkoff/Kushner envoy visit lapsed on schedule 8 Sep: Russia launched roughly 166 drones, 32 cruise missiles, and ballistic/anti-ship missiles at Kyiv overnight, killing at least 2-3 in the capital (5 nationwide, 63 injured) and damaging a TV newsroom, a school, and residential buildings.
bluf.matters: NATO Secretary-General Rutte said civilian deaths in Ukraine are at their highest level since May 2022, underscoring the pause's narrow, capital-only, time-boxed nature.
bluf.changes: Confirms the base-case forecast (pause lapses absent a broader framework) even as a separate, narrower energy-infrastructure-specific halt from the 7 Sep Trump-Putin call remains unconfirmed as violated -- the two commitments should be tracked separately.
bluf.needToKnow: The 8 Sep targets (TV station, homes, school) were not specifically energy infrastructure; do not conflate the lapsed capital pause with the still-unresolved energy-halt question.

bluf.what: CISA added four new CVEs to the KEV catalog on 8 Sep during a record Microsoft Patch Tuesday (~966-974 CVEs, 2 zero-days): CVE-2026-81963 (Windows Update Stack link-following elevation-of-privilege -- the first-ever exploited flaw in that specific component), CVE-2026-85880 (Windows ALPC heap-based buffer overflow EoP), CVE-2026-86218 (N-able N-central static code injection), and CVE-2026-75650 (the Adobe Commerce/Magento StyleSmuggler RCE already patched 7 Sep) was formally KEV-listed.
bluf.matters: Both Windows flaws grant SYSTEM-level privilege escalation and were exploited as zero-days before patches existed; N-able N-central is an RMM platform used by many MSPs, making it a supply-chain-relevant target.
bluf.changes: New confirmed in-the-wild exploitation in core Windows components, on top of the already-tracked edge/CI-CD/e-commerce cohort.
bluf.needToKnow: Prioritize the September Patch Tuesday rollout and N-able N-central patching on BOD 26-04 timelines; MikroTik's 'MikroTrick' chain remains actively exploited and still unlisted.

bluf.what: CMMC Phases 2-4 remain suspended with no new substance; the DoW CIO's internal Reform Task Force determination, previously targeted for ~13 Sep, is now roughly four days away, with the public report still expected ~28 Sep.
bluf.matters: The decision window is close enough that contractors should be in final readiness posture, not a holding pattern.
bluf.changes: No new information; time-to-decision has simply shortened further.
bluf.needToKnow: Continue treating this as a maintenance-posture decision, not a reason to stand down 800-171 controls.

bluf.what: The 24 Sep Trump-Xi White House visit remains the U.S.-side plan (Xi reportedly arriving 23 Sep, departing 25 Sep, coinciding with UNGA), with an agenda spanning trade/investment, AI, the Iran war, and Taiwan; Beijing has not formally confirmed the visit.
bluf.matters: A single meeting now sits at the intersection of nearly every major thread this brief series tracks -- rare-earth controls, Taiwan pressure, and the Iran conflict could all move on or around this date.
bluf.changes: No material change in status, but the date is close enough (two weeks out) to warrant active tracking.
bluf.needToKnow: Formal Chinese confirmation of the visit is the next hard indicator.

bluf.what: A previously under-tracked 13 Aug presidential memorandum ordering the Navy to plan replacing the Electromagnetic Aircraft Launch System (EMALS) with steam catapults on CVN-81 (the future USS Doris Miller), alongside a fifth public shipyard, additional submarine drydocks, and greater use of foreign shipyards for auxiliaries, remains a live schedule and cost risk not previously covered in this series.
bluf.matters: Naval architects and several outlets have called the EMALS-to-steam reversal technically regressive; the directive could add billions in cost and push CVN-81 delivery into the late 2030s.
bluf.changes: New to this brief series; the Secretary of War's required 60-day implementation plan (due roughly mid-October) is the next milestone.
bluf.needToKnow: Relevant to any organization in the carrier-systems, launch/recovery, or shipyard-infrastructure supply chain.

bluf.what: DoD's rollout of custom ChatGPT and Grok instances on GenAI.mil (reaching roughly 3 million personnel) continues even as Anthropic's Claude remains the only major model excluded from the platform; Pentagon leadership has reaffirmed the planned removal of Anthropic's products from DoD systems will complete by month-end.
bluf.matters: Illustrates that DoD's AI-adoption pace and its unresolved vendor-guardrail dispute with Anthropic are proceeding on separate, non-intersecting tracks.
bluf.changes: No new legal development since the 28 Aug district-court ruling; operationally, the ChatGPT/Grok rollout is now the more concrete near-term fact.
bluf.needToKnow: Watch the D.C. Circuit docket, not the platform rollout, for the dispute's actual resolution.

items.headline: Kyiv capital-strike pause lapses on schedule with a mass Russian attack; narrower energy-infrastructure halt status unresolved
items.observation: KNOWN (Ukrainian air force, Kyiv Independent, Bloomberg, ABC): Russia launched roughly 166 drones, 32 cruise missiles, and ballistic/anti-ship missiles at Kyiv overnight 7-8 Sep as the 5 Sep, 3-day capital-strike pause (tied to the Witkoff/Kushner envoy visit) ended; at least 2-3 were killed in Kyiv (5 nationwide, 63 injured), with a TV newsroom, a school, and residential buildings damaged. NATO Secretary-General Rutte said Ukrainian civilian deaths are now at their highest level since May 2022. REPORTED: a separate, narrower 30-day energy-infrastructure-specific strike halt from the 7 Sep Trump-Putin call, contingent on Ukrainian reciprocity, was not confirmed as violated by the 8 Sep strikes, whose targets were not specifically power/grid infrastructure.
items.context: The capital pause was always a narrow, time-boxed, envoy-visit-linked mechanism distinct from the broader energy-halt commitment reported two days later.
items.change: From an active pause to a resumed mass attack -- but on the capital-strike track, not necessarily the energy-infrastructure track.
items.significance: Confirms the prior cycle's base-case forecast (pause lapses absent a broader framework) while leaving the separate, potentially more durable energy-halt commitment's status genuinely open.
items.causation: The pause's term (tied to the envoy visit) simply expired; the visit produced no broader breakthrough per Zelensky's own comments.
items.actorIntent: ASSESSED: Russia used the capital pause as a low-cost gesture during the envoy visit while preserving offensive tempo elsewhere and holding the energy-halt question in reserve as a separate negotiating lever.
items.implications: No near-term drawdown in European air-defense or munitions demand; the war's kinetic tempo outside the two narrow pause categories remains fully active.
items.secondOrder: Sustained pull-through for air defense, counter-UAS, and munitions replenishment.

list: A confirmed strike specifically on Ukrainian power/grid infrastructure (would resolve the energy-halt question)
Any formal Ukrainian reciprocity confirmation on the energy halt
Further capital-area strikes outside any renewed pause

items.orgImpact: Industry-level: continuity of A&D demand; no organization-specific implication asserted.
items.myImpact: No direct enterprise-tech action; relevant as macro demand context.
items.takeaway: Don't conflate the lapsed capital pause with the separate energy-halt commitment -- only a specifically grid-targeted strike (or its absence) resolves the latter.

items.headline: Presidential memorandum orders EMALS-to-steam-catapult reversal for CVN-81, new public shipyard, more submarine drydocks
items.observation: KNOWN (multiple outlets, White House memorandum reporting): a 13 Aug National Security Presidential Memorandum directs the Secretary of War, within 60 days, to deliver a plan replacing the Electromagnetic Aircraft Launch System (EMALS) and Advanced Weapons Elevators with steam and hydraulic systems for CVN-81 (the future USS Doris Miller), already under construction at HII Newport News. The broader memorandum also directs planning for a fifth public shipyard near the Pacific Fleet, up to three additional submarine drydocks, a new component repair center, and greater use of foreign shipyards for auxiliary/warship construction with technology transfer back to U.S. yards.
items.context: Not previously covered in this brief series; the 60-day implementation-plan deadline falls in roughly mid-October.
items.change: A concrete, dated planning deadline is now approaching for a policy that naval architects have called technically regressive.
items.significance: Could add billions to CVN-81's cost and delay delivery into the late 2030s; reopens a design question (EMALS vs. steam) considered settled since the Ford class was conceived.
items.actorIntent: ASSESSED: administration priority on visible industrial-base expansion (new shipyard, drydocks, foreign-yard use) bundled with a specific technical reversal favored by the President personally.
items.implications: Schedule and cost risk for CVN-81; potential opportunity in steam/hydraulic catapult and elevator subsystems; broader shipyard-expansion demand.
items.secondOrder: A foreign-shipyard-construction provision would be a notable shift in U.S. Navy procurement practice if implemented.

list: The Secretary of War's required 60-day implementation plan (~mid-Oct)
Any CVN-81 cost/schedule restatement
Foreign-shipyard-use solicitations or agreements

items.orgImpact: Relevant to shipbuilding, launch/recovery-systems, and shipyard-infrastructure suppliers; a genuine schedule/cost risk to track on CVN-81-adjacent work.
items.myImpact: If any carrier-systems or shipyard-infrastructure work is in scope, flag this directive for program-risk review now, ahead of the mid-October plan.
items.takeaway: A one-month-old but still-unfolding directive with a concrete near-term deadline -- worth a dedicated look when the implementation plan lands.

items.headline: Army selects Teledyne FLIR's Rogue 1 for LASSO loitering-munition program; SES wins 5-year Ku-band BPA
items.observation: REPORTED: the Army selected Teledyne FLIR's Rogue 1 for the Lethal Miniature Aerial Missile System (LASSO) loitering-munition program, putting man-portable precision anti-armor strike capability into infantry brigade combat teams. items.headline: CISA adds two actively-exploited Windows zero-days plus N-able N-central to KEV amid record Patch Tuesday
items.threat: Local privilege escalation to SYSTEM via core Windows components (Update Stack, ALPC), exploited as zero-days before patches existed; separately, static code injection in a widely deployed MSP/RMM platform.
items.observedActivity: KNOWN (Microsoft, Tenable, BleepingComputer): September 2026 Patch Tuesday shipped roughly 966-974 CVE fixes, including two exploited-in-the-wild zero-days -- CVE-2026-81963 (Windows Update Stack link-following EoP, the first-ever exploited flaw in that specific component) and CVE-2026-85880 (Windows ALPC heap-based buffer overflow EoP). CISA added both to KEV the same day, alongside CVE-2026-86218 (N-able N-central static code injection) and a formal KEV listing for the already-patched Adobe Commerce/Magento StyleSmuggler flaw (CVE-2026-75650).
items.affected: Windows Update Stack (all supported Windows versions); Windows ALPC subsystem; N-able N-central RMM platform; Adobe Commerce/Magento (already patched via APSB26-146).
items.exploitation: Actively exploited (in KEV) for all four.
items.observation: KNOWN: CISA's 8 Sep KEV alert lists all four additions with active-exploitation evidence per BOD 26-04.
items.change: New confirmed in-the-wild exploitation in core Windows privilege-escalation paths, expanding beyond the edge/CI-CD/e-commerce cohort tracked in prior cycles.
items.significance: Windows Update Stack and ALPC are present on effectively every managed Windows endpoint; N-able N-central compromise can cascade across every client an MSP manages, making it a supply-chain-relevant target.
items.actorIntent: ASSESSED: opportunistic exploitation of newly disclosed zero-days consistent with a race between disclosure and patch adoption, rather than a single targeted campaign.
items.secondOrder: MSP/RMM compromise (N-able N-central) can propagate to downstream client networks, including DIB-adjacent managed environments.

list: Patch-adoption telemetry for the September release
Any N-able N-central compromise reports affecting downstream MSP clients
KEV listing of the still-unlisted MikroTik 'MikroTrick' chain

items.defenseRelevance: High -- Windows endpoints are near-universal in DIB networks, and MSP/RMM platforms are common in smaller contractor environments subject to DFARS 7012 safeguarding.
items.posture: Deploy the September Patch Tuesday updates immediately, prioritizing CVE-2026-81963 and CVE-2026-85880; patch N-able N-central to the fixed version; confirm Magento/Commerce credential rotation is complete; continue hunting for the MikroTik '-2' SSH-account IOC pending its KEV listing.
items.orgImpact: Immediate patch cycle for the September release plus N-able N-central; verify DFARS 7012 safeguarding-control evidence for all four newly listed CVEs.
items.myImpact: Own the September Patch Tuesday rollout as this week's top security-operations priority alongside the still-open MikroTik hunt.
items.takeaway: Two SYSTEM-level Windows zero-days now under active exploitation, plus a supply-chain-relevant RMM flaw -- patch this week, don't wait for the next cycle.

items.headline: Iran claims strikes on two U.S. destroyers; CENTCOM denies as Hormuz blacklist and price/volume divergence both deepen
items.observedAction: REPORTED/CLAIMED (IRGC via Iranian state media, 8 Sep): the IRGC claimed it struck two U.S. Navy destroyers and multiple oil tankers/vessels in retaliation for earlier U.S. strikes. KNOWN (CENTCOM): the claim is 'completely FALSE' -- no U.S. warship was hit and all IRGC attempted attacks failed; CENTCOM separately confirmed it had destroyed five more Iranian tankers in the same exchange (CENTCOM Commander Adm. Brad Cooper: 'If you shoot at two of our ships, we will impose an even higher economic cost'). Iran's Persian Gulf Strait Authority has expanded its Hormuz vessel blacklist to roughly 56-57 ships (from 45 on 24 Aug); commercial transit has fallen to ~10 ships/day, the lowest since May; Brent holds near a seven-week high (~$99/bbl).
items.likelyObjective: Sustain coercive pressure and preserve the 'faster, heavier, more painful' retaliation narrative even where kinetic attempts fail, while using the PGSA's existing permit/blacklist authority (in place since May 2026) as a lower-cost, non-kinetic lever that keeps tightening independent of any single strike's outcome.
items.capability: Demonstrated: repeated attempted strikes on U.S. and commercial vessels since late August, none confirmed by CENTCOM to have hit a U.S. warship; the PGSA blacklist/permit mechanism is an operating, demonstrated administrative capability, not merely declared intent.
items.intentAssessment: ASSESSED: a calculated, two-track escalation -- attempting harder kinetic targets (warships) while simultaneously tightening an already-functioning administrative-coercion tool -- consistent with substituting lower-cost levers as higher-cost ones (mine warfare, successful tanker strikes) are degraded or fail.
items.observation: CLAIMED via Iranian state media for the strike; KNOWN via CENTCOM for the denial and the tanker-destruction claim; REPORTED via shipping-data aggregators (cited by Reuters) for transit volumes.
items.change: First reported Iranian attempt to directly target U.S. Navy vessels (as opposed to tankers) in this cycle, alongside continued, measurable blacklist expansion.
items.significance: Raises the ceiling on miscalculation risk even where individual attempts fail, because the attempt itself signals a willingness to engage U.S. military assets directly.

list: Independent (non-Iranian, non-U.S.) confirmation of what actually happened 8 Sep
Any further attempted strike on a U.S. Navy vessel
PGSA blacklist count and Hormuz transit-volume trend
Any US/CENTCOM shift from denial to a more forceful public posture

items.orgImpact: Industry-level: energy-sector and shipping-dependent organizations should treat the claim/denial dynamic itself as a risk indicator, not just the underlying facts -- both sides have incentive to shape the narrative.
items.myImpact: If any Gulf-transiting logistics or energy exposure exists, this is a same-day leadership-briefing update; expect follow-up questions on what 'CENTCOM denies' actually tells us about ground truth.
items.takeaway: Whether or not the 8 Sep strikes actually hit anything, Iran is now attempting direct engagement with U.S. warships while simultaneously tightening an already-real administrative chokehold on Hormuz transit -- both dimensions warrant contingency planning now.

weakSignals.whyUnusual: Prior IRGC actions in this cycle focused on tankers and commercial shipping; a claimed direct hit on U.S. Navy combatants is a different risk category regardless of whether it is confirmed.

weakSignals.whyUnusual: A presidentially directed reversal of a design choice generally considered settled since Ford-class conception, moving from announcement to a dated implementation-plan requirement.

adImpact: This cycle's throughline is that the two dominant acute-risk threads both sharpened in the same direction -- Hormuz risk deepened as Iran claimed (and CENTCOM denied) direct strikes on U.S. Navy vessels while its transit-permit blacklist and falling commercial-transit volumes provided independently verifiable evidence of real-world strain, and Ukraine's diplomatic pause lapsed on schedule with a mass resumed attack on Kyiv even as a separate, narrower energy-infrastructure commitment's status remains genuinely open. On cyber, the picture widened rather than resolved: a record Patch Tuesday added two SYSTEM-level Windows zero-days and a supply-chain-relevant MSP/RMM flaw to KEV, on top of the still-unlisted MikroTik chain and last cycle's Magento/Commerce remediation work. The structural constraints tracked across recent cycles -- the rare-earth/magnet chokepoint, CMMC's now-imminent decision window, and the DoD-Anthropic AI-vendor dispute -- carried forward largely unchanged, even as a newly surfaced Navy shipbuilding directive (EMALS-to-steam reversal, foreign-yard use, a fifth public shipyard) adds a fresh schedule/cost risk and a third demand vector onto the same constrained magnet supply base. Net: assurance and supply-chain work remains the decisive variable for defense-sector organizations, and this cycle is a reminder that claim/denial dynamics in an active conflict (Iran-U.S.) deserve the same analytic skepticism applied to any single-sourced claim, regardless of which side is making it.

wrongAbout: We treat the 8 Sep Iranian strike claim as most likely unsuccessful/exaggerated (per CENTCOM) -- but if independent reporting later confirms a hit, we would be underweighting a genuine escalation already in progress.

We treat the lapsed Kyiv capital pause and the separate energy-infrastructure halt as analytically distinct -- but if reporting later shows Russia and Ukraine themselves treated them as one commitment, our distinction would be a false precision that obscures a simpler 'ceasefire collapsed' read.

We assess the CVN-81 steam-catapult reversal as a genuine, proceeding cost/schedule risk -- but if the mid-October plan quietly narrows scope or slips indefinitely, we would be overweighting a directive that may not survive programmatic review.

redTeam.issue: Significance of Iran's claimed strikes on U.S. Navy vessels
redTeam.objection: IRGC claims of striking U.S. assets have occurred before in this conflict cycle and have not previously been independently verified or led to a direct U.S.-Iran military engagement; treating this claim as CRITICAL may overweight Iranian information operations designed to project strength domestically and regionally.
redTeam.response: Valid caution, which is why the item is tagged CLAIMED/UNKNOWN on the strike itself and confidence is MODERATE rather than HIGH. But CENTCOM's own confirmation that Iran attempted the attacks (even if unsuccessful), combined with independently verifiable market behavior (falling transit volumes, sustained elevated oil prices) that does not depend on either side's claims, is why this remains CRITICAL priority for org-level contingency planning regardless of whether the specific 8 Sep claim is ever independently confirmed.

assumptions.assumption: The recipient is a senior enterprise-technology/cybersecurity/compliance leader in an aerospace/defense organization.
assumptions.impactIfWrong: Personal-relevance framing would need re-tailoring; the intelligence itself is unaffected.

assumptions.assumption: Open-source web-search summaries are reliable enough as leads when cited to named primaries (CISA, CENTCOM, named outlets/CERTs).
assumptions.whyRequired: This brief was compiled from a live OSINT sweep rather than direct document review; direct access to some primary sites (CISA.gov, several major news domains) was intermittently unavailable during compilation.
assumptions.impactIfWrong: Specific figures (exact strike counts, precise blacklist totals) could be imprecise; consequential claims are flagged by confidence and sourced to named outlets.

intelGaps: Independent (non-Iranian, non-U.S.) confirmation of what actually occurred in the 8 Sep Hormuz exchange.
Whether the separate 30-day energy-infrastructure strike-halt commitment has been formally, publicly reciprocated by Ukraine or violated by either side.
The exact scope and content of the Secretary of War's forthcoming CVN-81 implementation plan.

Direct access to cisa.gov, several major news domains (CNBC, Al Jazeera, NPR, ABC News), and the CISA KEV catalog itself was unavailable during this compilation; KEV-addition claims rely on secondary/aggregator and vendor-blog reporting and should be re-verified against the primary catalog.
competing: Hormuz 8 Sep exchange: a 'failed Iranian attempt, successfully deterred' reading (per CENTCOM) vs. a 'partially successful but downplayed' reading -- unresolved absent independent confirmation.

Ukraine: a 'ceasefire diplomacy effectively collapsed' reading vs. a 'narrower energy-specific channel still alive' reading -- both plausible given the capital pause's clean lapse and the energy halt's unconfirmed status.
confidenceLimits: Direct access to CISA's KEV catalog and several major news domains was unavailable during this compilation; several claims rely on secondary/aggregator reporting.
Casualty figures for the 8 Sep Kyiv attack varied across outlets (2-3 killed in Kyiv per some reports, 5 nationwide per others); treat as approximate and developing.
whatWouldChange: Independent confirmation or refutation of the 8 Sep Hormuz strike claim would sharpen that assessment from MODERATE to HIGH confidence.
A confirmed, specifically energy/grid-targeted Russian strike (or its continued absence over the coming week) would resolve the Ukraine energy-halt forecast.
Release of the Secretary of War's CVN-81 implementation plan would clarify the actual cost/schedule scope of the steam-catapult reversal.

forecastReview.priorForecast: Iran will follow through on its threatened 'faster, heavier, more painful' response with at least one further strike on a U.S.-linked or U.S.-flagged vessel or asset within 30 days.
forecastReview.note: The IRGC claimed strikes on two U.S. Navy destroyers and multiple tankers on 8 Sep, matching the threatened escalation in kind and target selection -- but CENTCOM says the attempts failed and no U.S. vessel was hit, so the attempt is confirmed while the outcome is denied.

forecastReview.priorForecast: The reported 30-day Ukraine energy-infrastructure strike-halt commitment will not hold cleanly for its full term without at least one contested violation claim from either side.
forecastReview.note: The separate capital-strike pause lapsed 8 Sep with a mass attack on Kyiv, but the targets (TV station, homes, school) were not specifically energy/grid infrastructure, so the narrower energy-halt commitment's status remains unconfirmed as violated.

forecastReview.priorForecast: The DoW CIO's internal CMMC Reform Task Force determination (~13 Sep) will recommend resuming assessment scaling on a revised timeline rather than a further indefinite pause or repeal.
forecastReview.note: Determination window now roughly four days out; no new substance to update the assessment.

forecastReview.priorForecast: Iran will formally publish and attempt to enforce the Hormuz-adjacent 'exclusion zone,' but will not succeed in materially reducing U.S.-escorted commercial transit volumes within 30 days.
forecastReview.note: The PGSA blacklist has grown to ~56-57 vessels and overall commercial transit has fallen to a post-May low (~10 ships/day), but it is unclear from reporting reviewed whether this reflects zone enforcement specifically versus broader conflict risk-avoidance, or whether it affects U.S.-escorted transit specifically.
